questions.q: What question does Rakesh ask at the very end of the story as he looks at the grown cherry tree?
questions.a: Rakesh asks, "Is this what it feels like to be God?" If a student answers that he asks when the tree will bear sweeter fruit or how many cherries grew, it reveals that the student is focusing only on the physical tree and has missed the character's climactic realization of creative wonder.

questions.q: Why is Rakesh's joy at the tree's survival different from the pleasure of simply buying cherries from the bazaar?
questions.a: Buying cherries provides only momentary physical satisfaction (taste), whereas watching the tree survive builds a personal, emotional bond because Rakesh invested time, patience, and care through its struggles. If a student says it is different because home-grown cherries are cheaper or taste sweeter, they misunderstand the psychological depth of nurturing and reduce life to a transaction.

questions.q: A student writes: "Rakesh was rewarded because the tree finally gave him lots of sweet cherries to sell." Apply your understanding of the story's theme to correct this statement in two sentences.
questions.a: To correct this statement: "Rakesh's true reward was not commercial or culinary, as the tree bore only a few sour cherries initially. Instead, his reward was the wonder of having sheltered a living being from death and watching it blossom into a home for birds and insects." If a student merely edits the grammar without correcting the factual claim about the sour fruit and emotional reward, they fail to apply the thematic concept.

questions.q: Analyze how the two major disasters—the goat eating the leaves and the woman cutting the sapling in half—strengthen the theme of nurturing rather than defeating it.
questions.a: These disasters test and deepen Rakesh's commitment; each time the plant is mutilated, Rakesh experiences grief, which leads to active protective measures (like piling pebbles around it) and resilience. The tree's persistent rebirth alongside Rakesh's enduring hope proves that nurturing is an active struggle against odds, making the final survival far more meaningful. If a student answers that these events simply make the story longer or shows that goats are harmful, they are describing plot events without analyzing thematic function.

questions.q: Evaluate Grandfather's role: Did Grandfather give Rakesh the seed to plant because he wanted cherries, or to teach him a life lesson? Defend your position with evidence from their conversations.
questions.a: Grandfather advised planting it so it would be of "use" and bring "luck," showing he valued purposeful action over passive consumption; he never expressed a desire to harvest fruit. Furthermore, when the sapling was cut, Grandfather offered philosophical reassurance rather than anger, proving his focus was on teaching Rakesh patience and respect for life's resilience. If a student argues Grandfather just wanted fruit in the garden, they overlook Grandfather's retired, contemplative character and his role as a mentor.

questions.q: Create a brief four-line reflection that Rakesh might write in a personal diary on the evening he touches the tree's trunk, expressing what "nurturing" has taught him about life.
questions.a:
A strong response will express awe, responsibility, and interconnectedness:
"Today, resting my hand against its rough bark, I realized this tree breathes because I did not walk away when it was broken. It gave me no sweet harvest today, yet it gave me life itself. In helping it live, I found my own place under the sky." 
A weak response will focus solely on gardening tasks (e.g., "I will water it tomorrow so I can eat cherries next summer") and fails to capture the philosophical depth required at Class 8 level.
